l: The Book of Hosea, The Book of Hosea, Chapter 13
s: Chapter 13 describes the LORD's indictment of Ephraim and Israel for idolatry. Ephraim, once exalted, died through guilt over Baal, and the people made silver molten images and kissed calves. The LORD says he alone is God and savior, that he knew them in the wilderness, and that they forgot him once they were filled. He therefore threatens to attack them like a lion, leopard, and bereaved bear, and he recalls giving and removing a king in anger. The chapter ends with Ephraim's stored-up guilt, a drying east wind, and Samaria falling by the sword with horrific violence against its infants and pregnant women.

l: Ephraim, The Book of Hosea, Chapter 13
s: Ephraim was once exalted in Israel, but became guilty through Baal and died. His guilt and sin are stored up, he is likened to an unwise son who fails to come to the opening of the womb, and though fruitful among his brothers his spring and fountain will dry up under an east wind, and his storehouse of treasure will be plundered.

l: Israel, The Book of Hosea, Chapter 13
s: Israel is accused of sinning more and more with idols and of forgetting the LORD after being filled in pasture. The LORD says Israel is destroyed because it is against him, its helper, and asks where its king and judges are to save it.

l: the LORD, The Book of Hosea, Chapter 13
s: The LORD declares he has been Israel's God since Egypt, that there is no savior besides him, and that he knew them in the wilderness. He announces he will act like a lion, leopard, and bereaved bear against them, speaks of ransoming from Sheol and death while saying compassion will be hidden from his eyes, and sends an east wind, his breath, to dry up Ephraim.

l: Samaria, The Book of Hosea, Chapter 13
s: Samaria will bear her guilt because she has rebelled against her God. Its people will fall by the sword, its infants will be dashed in pieces, and its pregnant women will be ripped open.

l: molten images and idols (Ephraim's idols), The Book of Hosea, Chapter 13
s: The people made molten images of their silver, idols according to their own understanding and the work of craftsmen. It is said of them that people offer human sacrifice and kiss the calves.

l: king (Israel's king), The Book of Hosea, Chapter 13
s: The LORD asks where Israel's king is now to save them in all their cities, recalling that the people asked for a king and princes. He says he gave a king in his anger and took him away in his wrath.

l: Israel's judgment and destruction, The Book of Hosea, Chapter 13
s: The people will pass away like morning mist, dew, chaff in the whirlwind, and smoke. The LORD will lurk and tear them like a lion, leopard, and bear, send a drying east wind, and bring the sword, infant killing, and ripping open of pregnant women on Samaria.

l: The Book of Hosea, The Book of Hosea, Chapter 14
s: Chapter 14 is a closing call for Israel to return to the LORD their God after falling because of their sin. It supplies words of repentance: asking forgiveness, offering vowed bulls, renouncing reliance on Assyria, horses, and the work of their hands as gods. The LORD then promises to heal their waywardness, love them freely, and turn away his anger. He likens himself to dew that makes Israel blossom, spread roots and branches, and shelter people who flourish like grain and vine. The LORD asks Ephraim what it has to do with idols, and the chapter ends by asking who is wise enough to understand that the LORD's ways are right, with the righteous walking in them and the rebellious stumbling.

l: the LORD, The Book of Hosea, Chapter 14
s: The LORD calls Israel to return and promises to heal their waywardness, love them freely, and turn his anger away. He compares himself to dew and to a green cypress tree, says Ephraim's fruit comes from him, and his ways are declared right, with the righteous walking in them and the rebellious stumbling.

l: Israel, The Book of Hosea, Chapter 14
s: Israel is told to return to the LORD because it has fallen through its sin, and is given words to say asking forgiveness and renouncing Assyria, horses, and handmade gods. The LORD promises it restoration: it will blossom like the lily, root like Lebanon, spread branches, and have beauty like the olive tree and fragrance like Lebanon.

l: Ephraim, The Book of Hosea, Chapter 14
s: Ephraim is addressed by the LORD, who asks what he has to do any more with idols. The LORD says he answers and will take care of Ephraim, and that Ephraim's fruit is found in him.

l: idols, The Book of Hosea, Chapter 14
s: The people are to stop calling the work of their hands 'Our gods.' The LORD asks Ephraim what he has to do any more with idols.

l: sin, The Book of Hosea, Chapter 14
s: Sin is named as the reason Israel has fallen. Israel is to ask the LORD to forgive all their sins, and the LORD responds by promising to heal their waywardness and turn away his anger.

l: The Book of Amos, The Book of Amos, The Book of Amos / Chapter 1
s: Chapter 1 of Amos introduces Amos, a herdsman of Tekoa, who saw his words concerning Israel in the days of Uzziah king of Judah and Jeroboam son of Joash king of Israel, two years before the earthquake. He declares that the LORD will roar from Zion and Jerusalem, causing the shepherds' pastures to mourn and Carmel's top to wither. The LORD then pronounces judgments on Damascus, Gaza, Tyre, Edom, and Ammon, each introduced by the formula 'for three transgressions, yes, for four, I will not turn away its punishment.' Each nation is charged with a specific wrong, such as threshing Gilead, delivering captives to Edom, forgetting a brotherly covenant, pursuing a brother with the sword, or ripping open pregnant women of Gilead. For each, the LORD promises fire that will devour its palaces, along with captivity or the cutting off of rulers and inhabitants.

l: Amos, The Book of Amos, The Book of Amos / Chapter 1
s: Amos is identified as one of the herdsmen of Tekoa, who saw the words of this book concerning Israel in the days of Uzziah and Jeroboam, two years before the earthquake. He relays that the LORD will roar from Zion and utter his voice from Jerusalem.

l: the LORD, The Book of Amos, The Book of Amos / Chapter 1
s: The LORD roars from Zion and speaks from Jerusalem, and pronounces judgment on Damascus, Gaza, Tyre, Edom, and Ammon. For each he declares he will not turn away punishment and will send fire to devour palaces, with captivity or the cutting off of rulers for some.

l: Damascus, The Book of Amos, The Book of Amos / Chapter 1
s: Damascus is condemned for threshing Gilead with iron threshing instruments. The LORD says he will send fire into the house of Hazael to devour the palaces of Ben Hadad, break the bar of Damascus, and send the people of Syria into captivity to Kir.

l: Gaza, The Book of Amos, The Book of Amos / Chapter 1
s: Gaza is condemned for carrying away captive the whole community to deliver them up to Edom. The LORD says he will send fire on its wall to devour its palaces, and will cut off the inhabitant from Ashdod and the scepter-holder from Ashkelon, turn his hand against Ekron, and cause the remnant of the Philistines to perish.

l: Edom, The Book of Amos, The Book of Amos / Chapter 1
s: Edom receives captives delivered up by Gaza and Tyre. Edom itself is condemned for pursuing his brother with the sword, casting off all pity, and keeping his anger and wrath forever, and the LORD says he will send fire on Teman to devour the palaces of Bozrah.

l: Tyre, The Book of Amos, The Book of Amos / Chapter 1
s: Tyre is condemned for delivering up the whole community to Edom and not remembering the brotherly covenant. The LORD says he will send fire on its wall to devour its palaces.

l: Ammon, The Book of Amos, The Book of Amos / Chapter 1
s: The children of Ammon are condemned for ripping open the pregnant women of Gilead in order to enlarge their border. The LORD says he will kindle fire in the wall of Rabbah to devour its palaces, amid shouting and storm in battle, and their king and princes will go into captivity together.

l: punishment, The Book of Amos, The Book of Amos / Chapter 1
s: Punishment is announced for each nation with the formula 'for three transgressions, yes, for four, I will not turn away its punishment.' It takes the form of fire devouring palaces, along with captivity and the cutting off of rulers and inhabitants.

l: The Book of Amos, The Book of Amos, Chapter 2
s: In Chapter 2 the LORD pronounces judgment on three nations using the formula "for three transgressions, yes, for four." Moab will be consumed by fire, its palaces of Kerioth devoured, and its judge and princes killed, because it burned the bones of the king of Edom into lime. Judah will suffer fire on the palaces of Jerusalem because it rejected the LORD's law and statutes and was led astray by lies. The longest section concerns Israel, accused of selling the righteous and needy, trampling the poor, sexual misuse of a maiden, and profaning holy places, despite the LORD destroying the Amorite, bringing them out of Egypt, and raising prophets and Nazirites whom they corrupted and silenced. The LORD declares he will crush Israel like a loaded cart, and neither the swift, strong, mighty, archer, nor horseman will escape.

l: the LORD, The Book of Amos, Chapter 2
s: The LORD announces that he will not turn away punishment for the transgressions of Moab, Judah, and Israel. He recalls destroying the Amorite, bringing Israel out of Egypt and through forty years in the wilderness, and raising up prophets and Nazirites. He declares he will send fire on Moab and Judah and crush Israel.

l: Moab, The Book of Amos, Chapter 2
s: Moab is condemned because it burned the bones of the king of Edom into lime. The LORD will send fire to devour the palaces of Kerioth, and Moab will die amid tumult, shouting, and trumpet sound, with its judge and all its princes killed.

l: Judah, The Book of Amos, Chapter 2
s: Judah is condemned for rejecting the LORD's law, not keeping his statutes, and being led astray by lies after which its fathers walked. The LORD will send fire on Judah that will devour the palaces of Jerusalem.

l: Israel, The Book of Amos, Chapter 2
s: Israel receives the longest indictment and is reminded of the LORD's past acts: destroying the Amorite, bringing them out of Egypt, leading them forty years, and raising up prophets and Nazirites. The people gave the Nazirites wine and commanded the prophets not to prophesy, and the LORD will crush them in their place.

l: Israel's transgressions and oppression of the poor, The Book of Amos, Chapter 2
s: Israel is accused of selling the righteous for silver and the needy for a pair of sandals, trampling the heads of the poor into the dust, and denying justice to the oppressed. A man and his father use the same maiden, profaning the LORD's holy name. They lie beside altars on garments taken in pledge and drink wine of those who have been fined in the house of their God.

l: coming judgment, The Book of Amos, Chapter 2
s: The judgment takes the form of fire on Moab and Judah and of crushing on Israel like a cart full of grain. For Israel, flight will fail the swift, the strong and mighty cannot save themselves, the archer will not stand, the fast runner and horseman will not escape, and even the courageous will flee naked on that day.

l: The Book of Amos, The Book of Amos, Chapter 3
s: The LORD addresses the children of Israel, the whole family He brought out of Egypt, declaring that because He chose them alone He will punish them for their sins. Through a series of rhetorical questions about lions, traps, and trumpets, the passage argues that disaster comes only by cause, that evil in a city is the LORD's doing, and that He reveals His plans to His servants the prophets, who must therefore prophesy. Ashdod and Egypt are summoned to assemble on the mountains of Samaria and witness its unrest and oppression, where people hoard plunder and loot in their palaces. The LORD announces that an adversary will overrun the land, pull down strongholds and plunder fortresses, and that only a remnant will be rescued, like scraps from a lion's mouth. He also promises to visit the altars of Bethel, cutting off their horns, and to strike the winter and summer houses so that the houses of ivory and the great houses perish.

l: the LORD, The Book of Amos, Chapter 3
s: The LORD speaks against the children of Israel, reminding them that He brought them out of Egypt and chose them alone of all earth's families, and so will punish their sins. He claims responsibility for evil that happens to a city, reveals His secrets to the prophets, and announces that He will bring an adversary, visit the altars of Bethel, and strike the winter and summer houses.

l: Israel, The Book of Amos, Chapter 3
s: The children of Israel are addressed as the whole family the LORD brought out of Egypt and chose above all earth's families, and are therefore to be punished for their sins. Those who sit at ease in Samaria on couches and silken cushions will be rescued only as a shepherd saves two legs or a piece of an ear from a lion's mouth.

l: Samaria, The Book of Amos, Chapter 3
s: Samaria's mountains are the place where Ashdod and Egypt are called to assemble and see the unrest and oppression within her. Its people, who hoard plunder and loot in their palaces, are described as not knowing how to do right, and those who sit on its couches and cushions will be barely rescued.

l: prophets (raised from Israel's sons), The Book of Amos, Chapter 3
s: The prophets are called the LORD's servants, to whom the Lord GOD reveals His secret before doing anything. Having heard the LORD speak like a roaring lion, the passage says they cannot help but prophesy.

l: adversary (against Israel), The Book of Amos, Chapter 3
s: An adversary is announced as coming to overrun the land. He will pull down the strongholds of Samaria's people and plunder their fortresses.

l: Israel's sins and oppression, The Book of Amos, Chapter 3
s: The text names Israel's sins as the reason for punishment, citing unrest and oppression in Samaria. The LORD says the people do not know to do right and hoard plunder and loot in their palaces, and He also refers to the transgressions of Israel and the altars of Bethel.

l: coming punishment and destruction, The Book of Amos, Chapter 3
s: The LORD promises that an adversary will overrun the land, pull down strongholds, and plunder fortresses, with only a scrap-like remnant rescued. On the day He visits Israel's transgressions, the horns of Bethel's altars will be cut off and fall, and the winter house, summer house, houses of ivory, and great houses will be struck down and come to an end.

l: The Book of Amos, The Book of Amos, Chapter 4
s: In this chapter the Lord GOD addresses the "cows of Bashan" on the mountain of Samaria, who oppress the poor and crush the needy while telling their husbands to bring them drinks. He swears by his holiness that they will be taken away with hooks and fish hooks and go out through breaks in the wall into Harmon. He sarcastically tells the children of Israel to go to Bethel and Gilgal to sin, and to bring sacrifices and free will offerings that please them. He then lists calamities he sent, including lack of bread, withheld rain, blight, mildew, locusts, plagues, sword, and overthrow like Sodom and Gomorrah, each followed by the refrain that Israel has not returned to him. The chapter closes with a call for Israel to prepare to meet its God, the LORD, the God of Armies, who forms the mountains and creates the wind.

l: the LORD, The Book of Amos, Chapter 4
s: The LORD, called the Lord GOD, swears by his holiness to take the cows of Bashan away with hooks and mocks Israel's worship at Bethel and Gilgal. He claims to have sent hunger, drought, blight, locusts, plagues, the sword, and overthrow, and he calls Israel to prepare to meet him. He is described as the one who forms the mountains, creates the wind, declares to man his thought, makes the morning darkness, and treads on the high places of the earth, named the God of Armies.

l: cows of Bashan, The Book of Amos, Chapter 4
s: The cows of Bashan, on the mountain of Samaria, are accused of oppressing the poor and crushing the needy while telling their husbands to bring them drinks. They are told that days will come when they are taken away with hooks, and they will go out through breaks in the wall, each straight ahead, and cast themselves into Harmon.

l: Israel, The Book of Amos, Chapter 4
s: Israel, addressed as the children of Israel, is told sarcastically to go to Bethel and Gilgal and sin, bringing sacrifices, tithes, leavened thanksgiving offerings, and boasted-about free will offerings that please them. It has suffered hunger, drought, blight, locusts, plagues, the sword, and overthrow, yet has not returned to the LORD, and is told to prepare to meet its God.

l: deportation with hooks, The Book of Amos, Chapter 4
s: The Lord GOD swears that days will come when the cows of Bashan are taken away with hooks, and the last of them with fish hooks. They will leave through breaks in the wall, each straight before her, and cast themselves into Harmon.

l: calamities sent against Israel, The Book of Amos, Chapter 4
s: The LORD lists cleanness of teeth and lack of bread, rain withheld three months before harvest and sent on one city but not another, blight and mildew, swarming locusts, plagues like Egypt's, young men slain by the sword, horses carried away, and an overthrow like Sodom and Gomorrah. Some were left like a burning stick plucked from the fire.

l: failure to return to the LORD, The Book of Amos, Chapter 4
s: After each calamity the LORD repeats that Israel has not returned to him, a refrain appearing in verses 6 through 11. Because of this, he tells Israel to prepare to meet its God.

l: The Book of Amos, The Book of Amos, Chapter 5
s: Chapter 5 opens with a lamentation over the house of Israel, declaring that the virgin of Israel has fallen and that its cities will be left with only a tenth of their men. The LORD urges Israel to seek him and live rather than seek Bethel, Gilgal, or Beersheba, and he is presented as the creator who brings sudden destruction on the strong. He condemns those who pervert justice, trample the poor, take bribes, and hate the one who reproves in the gate, promising that their stone houses and vineyards will not benefit them. He warns that the day of the LORD will be darkness, not light, rejects Israel's feasts, offerings, and songs, and calls for justice to roll on like rivers. The chapter ends with the LORD announcing captivity beyond Damascus.

l: the LORD, The Book of Amos, Chapter 5
s: The LORD calls Israel to seek him and live, and presents himself as the maker of the Pleiades and Orion who brings sudden destruction on the strong. He knows Israel's offenses, hates and rejects their feasts and offerings, and demands justice. He announces he will pass through the midst of Israel and send them into captivity beyond Damascus, and is named the God of Armies.

l: house of Israel, The Book of Amos, Chapter 5
s: The house of Israel is mourned in a lamentation as fallen, with its cities to be reduced to a tenth of their fighting men. It is accused of trampling the poor, taking bribes, and turning away the needy in the courts, and is told to seek good, hate evil, and establish justice so that the LORD may be gracious to the remnant of Joseph. Its punishment is wailing in the streets and vineyards and captivity beyond Damascus.

l: Bethel, The Book of Amos, Chapter 5
s: Bethel is named as a place Israel must not seek. The LORD says it will come to nothing, and that fire could break out in the house of Joseph with no one to quench it in Bethel.

l: Gilgal, The Book of Amos, Chapter 5
s: Gilgal is named with Bethel and Beersheba as a place Israel must not seek, enter, or pass to. The LORD declares it will surely go into captivity.

l: day of the LORD, The Book of Amos, Chapter 5
s: The day of the LORD is something Israel desires, but the LORD pronounces woe on those who long for it. He says it is darkness and not light, comparing it to a man who flees a lion and meets a bear, or leans on a wall at home and is bitten by a snake.

l: justice and righteousness, The Book of Amos, Chapter 5
s: Justice is turned to wormwood by those who cast righteousness to the earth, and it is denied in the courts through bribes and the rejection of the needy. The LORD commands Israel to establish justice in the courts and to let it roll on like rivers and righteousness like a mighty stream.

l: religious feasts and offerings, The Book of Amos, Chapter 5
s: The LORD says he hates and despises Israel's feasts and solemn assemblies. He will not accept their burnt offerings, meal offerings, or peace offerings, and he tells them to take away the noise of their songs and harps.

l: captivity, The Book of Amos, Chapter 5
s: Captivity is announced as the coming fate of Gilgal and of Israel. The LORD says he will cause the people to go into captivity beyond Damascus.

l: The Book of Amos, The Book of Amos, Chapter 6
s: Chapter 6 pronounces woe on the complacent notable men of Zion and Samaria, who feast, lounge on ivory beds, play music, and drink wine and anoint themselves with oils while not grieving for the affliction of Joseph. They are told to compare themselves with Calneh, Hamath, and Gath, and are accused of putting off the evil day and turning justice into poison. The LORD swears by himself that he abhors the pride of Jacob and will deliver up the city with all in it, so that they will go captive first and the feasting will end. Death will fill the houses, great and small, and survivors will not dare mention the LORD's name. The LORD announces he will raise up a nation against the house of Israel to afflict them from the entrance of Hamath to the brook of the Arabah.

l: the LORD, The Book of Amos, Chapter 6
s: The LORD, the God of Armies, swears by himself that he abhors the pride of Jacob and detests his fortresses, and so will deliver up the city with all that is in it. He commands that the great house be smashed to pieces and the little house into bits, and he declares he will raise up a nation against the house of Israel to afflict them.

l: house of Israel, The Book of Amos, Chapter 6
s: The house of Israel comes to its notable men, who are accused of turning justice into poison and the fruit of righteousness into bitterness. Addressed directly, it is told that the LORD will raise up a nation against it that will afflict it from the entrance of Hamath to the brook of the Arabah.

l: Samaria, The Book of Amos, Chapter 6
s: Samaria is named as a mountain on which the notable men feel secure, and they are the target of a woe. Its city, with all that is in it, will be delivered up by the LORD, and its houses will be struck down, great and little.

l: complacent elites (notable men of Zion and Samaria), The Book of Amos, Chapter 6
s: These men are described as at ease and secure, lying on ivory beds, eating choice lambs and calves, strumming harps, inventing instruments like David, drinking wine in bowls, and anointing themselves with the best oils, while not grieving for the affliction of Joseph. They put far away the evil day, boast of taking horns by their own strength, and are told they will go captive with the first who go captive, ending the feasting and lounging.

l: nation (raised up against Israel), The Book of Amos, Chapter 6
s: An unnamed nation is to be raised up by the LORD against the house of Israel. It will afflict Israel from the entrance of Hamath to the brook of the Arabah.

l: captivity (of Israel), The Book of Amos, Chapter 6
s: The notable men are told they will now go captive with the first who go captive, which ends their feasting and lounging. The text pairs this with the deaths in the houses and the afflicting of Israel by a raised-up nation.

l: The Book of Amos, The Book of Amos, Chapter 7
s: In Amos 7, the Lord GOD shows Amos three visions: locusts devouring the latter growth after the king's harvest, a judgment by fire that dries up the great deep, and the Lord standing by a wall with a plumb line. Amos pleads for Jacob after the first two visions and the LORD relents, but the plumb line signals that the LORD will no longer pass by Israel, with the high places of Isaac and the house of Jeroboam to fall by the sword. Amaziah the priest of Bethel reports to King Jeroboam that Amos is conspiring and tells Amos to flee to Judah and stop prophesying at the king's sanctuary. Amos answers that he was a herdsman and farmer of sycamore figs whom the LORD took to prophesy to Israel, and he pronounces judgment on Amaziah's family and land and repeats that Israel will be led away captive.

l: the LORD, The Book of Amos, Chapter 7
s: The Lord GOD shows Amos visions of locusts, judgment by fire, and a plumb line. He relents after Amos's pleas about the locusts and the fire, but declares he will set a plumb line among Israel and not pass by them again. He also pronounces judgment on Amaziah and his household.

l: Amos, The Book of Amos, Chapter 7
s: Amos receives three visions and twice pleads for Jacob, who is small, and the LORD relents. Accused by Amaziah of conspiracy and told to flee to Judah, he replies that he was no prophet nor a prophet's son but a herdsman and farmer of sycamore figs whom the LORD called. He then announces the LORD's judgment against Amaziah and repeats that Israel will be led away captive.

l: Amaziah, The Book of Amos, Chapter 7
s: Amaziah, priest of Bethel, sends word to Jeroboam that Amos has conspired against him and that the land cannot bear his words. He tells Amos to flee to Judah and not prophesy again at Bethel, the king's sanctuary. Amos declares that his wife will be a prostitute, his children will fall by the sword, his land will be divided, and he will die in an unclean land.

l: Jeroboam, The Book of Amos, Chapter 7
s: Jeroboam is king of Israel. The LORD says he will rise against the house of Jeroboam with the sword, and Amaziah reports that Amos says Jeroboam will die by the sword.

l: house of Israel, The Book of Amos, Chapter 7
s: Jacob is described by Amos as small in his pleas, asking how he could stand. Because of these pleas the LORD relents from the locusts and the fire.

l: Israel, The Book of Amos, Chapter 7
s: Israel is the LORD's people, in the midst of whom he will set a plumb line and not pass by again. Its sanctuaries will be laid waste, and it is said it will surely be led away captive out of its land. Amos is sent to prophesy to Israel, though Amaziah tells him to stop.

l: locusts, The Book of Amos, Chapter 7
s: In the first vision the LORD forms locusts at the start of the latter growth, after the king's harvest. They finish eating the grass of the land, prompting Amos's plea, and the LORD relents.

l: fire (judgment by fire), The Book of Amos, Chapter 7
s: In the second vision the Lord GOD calls for judgment by fire, which dries up the great deep and would have devoured the land. After Amos pleads, the LORD relents and says it shall not be.

l: plumb line, The Book of Amos, Chapter 7
s: In the third vision the Lord stands beside a wall made by a plumb line with a plumb line in his hand. He tells Amos he will set a plumb line in the middle of Israel and will not pass by them again, with desolation to follow.

l: The Book of Amos, The Book of Amos, Chapter 8
s: In Amos 8, the Lord GOD shows Amos a basket of summer fruit and declares that the end has come on his people Israel and he will no longer pass them by. He condemns those who swallow up the needy and poor, who wait for the new moon and Sabbath to pass so they can sell grain, cheating with a small ephah, a large shekel, and deceitful balances, and who buy the poor for silver and sell the sweepings with the wheat. The LORD swears by the pride of Jacob never to forget their works, and announces that the land will tremble, the sun will go down at noon, and feasts and songs will turn into mourning like that for an only son. He also promises a famine not of bread or water but of hearing the LORD's words, in which people wander from sea to sea without finding it, and the young faint from thirst. Those who swear by the sin of Samaria and by the gods of Dan and Beersheba will fall and never rise again.

l: the LORD, The Book of Amos, Chapter 8
s: The Lord GOD shows Amos a basket of summer fruit and explains that the end has come on Israel and he will not pass by them again. He swears by the pride of Jacob never to forget their works, and promises to darken the earth at noon, turn feasts into mourning, and send a famine of hearing his words.

l: Amos, The Book of Amos, Chapter 8
s: Amos is shown a vision of a basket of summer fruit and, when asked what he sees, answers correctly. He is then told by the Lord GOD that the end has come on Israel, and he delivers the message against those who oppress the needy.

l: Israel, The Book of Amos, Chapter 8
s: Israel is declared by the Lord GOD to have reached its end, with the LORD no longer passing by them. Its temple songs will become wailing, many dead bodies will be thrown out in silence, and its feasts will turn to mourning like that for an only son. Those who swear by the sin of Samaria, the god of Dan, and the way of Beersheba will fall and never rise again.

l: basket of summer fruit (Amos's vision), The Book of Amos, Chapter 8
s: The basket of summer fruit is what the Lord GOD shows Amos and what Amos names when asked what he sees. It serves as the sign that the end has come on Israel.

l: the needy and poor (oppressed by Israel's merchants), The Book of Amos, Chapter 8
s: The needy and poor are the ones whom the merchants desire to swallow up and cause to fail. They are bought for silver and for a pair of sandals, and are the object of the deceit the LORD swears never to forget.

l: exploitative merchants (addressed by Amos), The Book of Amos, Chapter 8
s: The merchants are told to hear that they long for the new moon and Sabbath to end so they can sell grain and wheat. They cheat with a small ephah, a large shekel, and deceitful balances, buy the poor for silver, and sell the sweepings with the wheat. The LORD swears never to forget any of their works.

l: famine of hearing the LORD's words, The Book of Amos, Chapter 8
s: The LORD announces a coming famine in the land that is not of bread or water but of hearing his words. People will wander from sea to sea and from north to east seeking the LORD's word and not find it, and the beautiful virgins and young men will faint for thirst in that day.

l: coming end and judgment on Israel, The Book of Amos, Chapter 8
s: The judgment is signaled by the basket of summer fruit and the declaration that the end has come. It includes the land trembling, the sun going down at noon, the earth darkened in clear day, feasts turned to mourning with sackcloth and baldness, and a bitter day like mourning for an only son.

l: dishonest trade practices, The Book of Amos, Chapter 8
s: The text describes making the ephah small, the shekel large, and dealing falsely with balances of deceit. It also includes selling the sweepings with the wheat and treating the Sabbath and new moon as obstacles to marketing grain. The LORD swears he will never forget such works.

l: The Book of Amos, The Book of Amos, Chapter 9
s: In Chapter 9 the speaker sees the Lord standing beside the altar commanding the striking of the pillars and promising that no one in the sinful kingdom will escape, whether they flee to Sheol, heaven, Carmel, the sea, or captivity. The Lord, described as the GOD of Armies who touches the land and builds his rooms in the heavens, says Israel is like the Ethiopians to him, yet he brought Israel from Egypt, the Philistines from Caphtor, and the Syrians from Kir. He will destroy the sinful kingdom but not utterly the house of Jacob, sifting Israel among the nations without losing a kernel, while the sinners of his people who deny that evil will reach them die by the sword. The chapter ends with the Lord promising to raise up David's fallen tent, bring Israel back from captivity, and plant them permanently in their land amid abundant harvests.

l: the LORD, The Book of Amos, Chapter 9
s: The Lord is seen standing beside the altar and commands the striking of the pillars, vowing to pursue all of the sinful with the sword and serpent wherever they hide. He is described as the GOD of Armies who melts the land by touching it, builds his rooms in the heavens, and calls the sea's waters onto the earth. He states that he brought up Israel from Egypt, the Philistines from Caphtor, and the Syrians from Kir, and promises to sift Israel, raise David's tent, and plant his people permanently in their land.

l: Israel, The Book of Amos, Chapter 9
s: Israel, called the children of Israel and the house of Jacob, is told it is like the Ethiopians to the Lord, who also brought it up from Egypt. The sinful kingdom is to be destroyed from the earth, but the house of Jacob will not be utterly destroyed and will be sifted among the nations without losing the least kernel. Israel is promised a return from captivity, rebuilt cities, vineyards, and gardens, and never again being plucked from the land the Lord gave.

l: sinners of my people, The Book of Amos, Chapter 9
s: The sinners of the Lord's people are those who say, 'Evil won't overtake nor meet us.' The Lord declares that all of them will die by the sword.

l: tent of David, The Book of Amos, Chapter 9
s: The tent of David is described as fallen, with breaches and ruins. The Lord promises that in that day he will raise it up, close its breaches, and build it as in the days of old, so that they may possess the remnant of Edom and all the nations called by his name.

l: restoration of Israel, The Book of Amos, Chapter 9
s: The Lord promises that days are coming when harvests will be so abundant that the plowman overtakes the reaper and sweet wine drips from the mountains. He will bring his people back from captivity, and they will rebuild ruined cities, inhabit them, plant vineyards, and make gardens. He says he will plant them on their land and they will no more be plucked up from it.

This document is the book of Exodus (chapters 1-40), narrating Israel's passage from Egyptian bondage to the establishment of worship at the tabernacle. The most important figures are the LORD (God), Moses, his brother Aaron, and Pharaoh, with supporting roles for Miriam, Jethro, Joshua, Bezalel and Oholiab. It begins with the Israelites multiplying in Egypt, a new king oppressing them with hard labor, and Pharaoh ordering newborn boys killed. Moses is hidden, rescued by Pharaoh's daughter, and raised as her son, then flees to Midian after killing an Egyptian, marrying Zipporah. At the burning bush, God reveals himself as 'I AM WHO I AM' and sends Moses, with Aaron as spokesman, to demand Israel's release. Pharaoh refuses and increases their burdens, and a series of plagues follows: blood, frogs, lice, flies, livestock pestilence, boils, hail, locusts, and darkness, with Pharaoh's heart repeatedly hardened. The final plague kills Egypt's firstborn, while Israel, marked by Passover lamb's blood, is spared and leaves, with ordinances for Unleavened Bread and the firstborn. Led by pillars of cloud and fire, Israel is pursued to the sea, which divides; Pharaoh's army drowns, and Moses and Miriam lead songs of praise. In the wilderness the people murmur over bitter water, hunger, and thirst, and God provides sweetened water, quail, manna with the Sabbath rest, and water from the rock; Israel defeats Amalek, and Jethro advises Moses to appoint judges. At Sinai, Israel agrees to the covenant, and God speaks the commandments, followed by detailed civil, moral, and religious laws, and the covenant is ratified with blood. Moses ascends the mountain for forty days, where God gives instructions for the tabernacle, ark, altars, priestly garments, consecration, incense, and anointing oil, and names Bezalel and Oholiab as craftsmen. Meanwhile the people have Aaron make a golden calf; Moses breaks the tablets, the Levites kill about three thousand, and Moses intercedes. God relents, renews the covenant on new tablets, reveals his merciful name, and Moses' face shines. The closing chapters describe the people's generous offerings, the craftsmen building everything as commanded, and Moses setting up the tabernacle in the second year's first month. The cloud covers the Tent and God's glory fills it, and Israel thereafter journeys only when the cloud lifts.

The Israelites, also called the children of Israel, are a numerous people who belong to the LORD, described as his son and firstborn. The records open with their bondage in Egypt, where Egyptians and taskmasters oppress them. They sigh and cry out, and God hears, remembering his covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. He promises to bring them to a good and large land. Their labor worsens when they must gather their own straw yet still meet the same brick quota, and their officers are beaten when it falls short. When Aaron speaks and performs the signs, they believe, and on hearing that the LORD has seen their affliction they bow and worship. They are spared the plagues that strike Egypt: none of their livestock dies, and no hail falls in Goshen, where they live. The LORD brings them out of Egypt with great power and a mighty hand. In the wilderness they gather around Moses to have disputes judged, and later are judged by appointed rulers. At the mountain they receive the commandments, including having no other gods before the LORD and honoring parents. Seeing the thunder, lightning, and smoke, they tremble, stay at a distance, and ask Moses to speak to them in place of God. They then accept the covenant, promising with one voice to do and obey all the LORD's words, and Moses sprinkles them with blood. The arc turns when Moses is delayed: they demand gods from Aaron, give up their gold, and worship a molded calf. Moses destroys the calf, about three thousand die, and the LORD strikes them. The LORD calls them stiff-necked and says he will not go up among them. They mourn and strip off their jewelry at his command. By the end they watch Moses go to the Tent and worship when the pillar of cloud descends. Overall, they are a chosen, rescued, and covenanted people whose fear, obedience, and worship alternate with serious failure.

The children of Israel are a people descended from the sons of Israel, including Reuben, who came into Egypt numbering seventy souls. They became fruitful, mighty and so numerous that the land was filled with them, and the Egyptians, who held them in bondage, came to dread them. They are called the LORD's people and armies, dwelling in Goshen, which the LORD set apart from the Egyptians; they had light in their dwellings during the darkness. Their central purpose is to serve the LORD, and Moses and Aaron demand their release. After 430 years in Egypt, they keep the Passover and leave in haste in the month Abib, about 600,000 men on foot besides children, armed, plundering the Egyptians, and encamping at Etham. They pass through the sea on dry ground, see the Egyptians dead, and believe in the LORD and Moses. In the wilderness they repeatedly murmur and quarrel over water and food, yet receive manna for forty years, water from the rock, and victory over Amalek at Rephidim. In the third month they reach the wilderness of Sinai and camp before the mountain, answering together that they will do all the LORD has spoken. They are offered status as his own possession, a kingdom of priests and a holy nation, conditional on obeying his voice and keeping his covenant. They receive laws: honest dealing, Sabbath and feasts (unleavened bread, weeks, harvest), redemption of the firstborn, no covenants with or bowing to other gods, and the half-shekel ransom. Moses calls them a stiff-necked people and asks pardon for them. Their names are borne on the priestly ephod and breastplate, and the LORD promises to dwell among them. They bring such abundant willing offerings for the sanctuary that Moses restrains them, then build the tabernacle according to all the LORD commanded. The account ends with them travelling only when the cloud lifts from the tabernacle, seeing the cloud by day and fire by night.

Egypt is a land on the Nile, described as the house of bondage, where the Israelites multiplied, were feared by a new king, and built the storage cities Pithom and Raamses for Pharaoh. Joseph was already there and Jacob's household came to join him. What matters most is that Egypt is the place of Israel's affliction and the stage for God's wonders leading to their release. The account unfolds as God announces he will bring his people out and strike Egypt with all his wonders. Moses, whose brothers remain there, returns after the men seeking his life are dead. Signs follow: the waters turn to blood; frogs, lice and flies afflict the land, though its magicians can imitate only the frogs; livestock pestilence, boils, and a hail with lightning worse than any since it became a nation strike it, while Goshen alone is spared. Locusts devour what the hail left, and thick darkness covers the land for three days. Pharaoh's servants call Egypt destroyed. The final plague comes at midnight, when all firstborn die, leaving no house without a dead, and an unprecedented great cry rises throughout the land. After Pharaoh stubbornly refused to release them, Israel leaves after 430 years, setting out from Rameses, brought out by the LORD's strength of hand.

Pharaoh is the king of Egypt, who rules the land, its servants, and commands taskmasters, an army, and chariots. He is introduced as a new king who did not know Joseph and who feared the numerous children of Israel might join enemies in war and leave. He set taskmasters over them and ordered newborn Hebrew boys cast into the river. Later Moses is sent to him; God says he will not give permission to go until God strikes Egypt with wonders, and that the LORD will harden his heart. Moses is to tell him to let Israel go or his firstborn son will be killed. Pharaoh says he does not know the LORD, refuses to release the people, calls their desire for a feast and sacrifice idleness, and worsens their burden by withholding straw while keeping the brick count. Through the plagues he is stubborn and unwilling to listen: he asks for a miracle, relies on his wise men and sorcerers, and bargains with offers to let them sacrifice in the land, send only the men, or send the little ones but keep the flocks. Under pressure he confesses sin and promises release, but each time relief comes he hardens his heart again, along with his servants. He finally orders Moses out on pain of death. At midnight his firstborn, who sat on his throne, is struck. Pharaoh rises in the night, calls Moses and Aaron, and tells them to take the Israelites, flocks and herds and go serve the LORD, asking for a blessing. He and his servants then regret the release; his heart is hardened by the LORD, and he takes his army and chariots to pursue Israel to the sea. There he, his chariots, horses and horsemen are overthrown, his chosen captains sunk in the Red Sea, and the LORD gains honor over him. His arc runs from fearful oppressor to defiant refuser, to a brief, coerced yielding, and finally to destruction.

The Egyptians are the people who dominate and oppress Israel in these records, and their story is one of escalating conflict ending in their ruin. They begin by dreading the multiplying Israelites, enslaving them ruthlessly with hard labor, and Pharaoh orders every Hebrew son thrown into the river. God promises deliverance and says the Egyptians will favor Israel, so Israelite women ask them for jewels and clothing. A series of plagues follows: the river turns to blood and cannot be drunk, livestock die, boils and hail strike, and some of Pharaoh's servants who fear the LORD's word shelter their servants and livestock while others do not. The LORD distinguishes them from Israel. The death of their firstborn causes a great cry; they urge Israel to leave in haste, saying "We are all dead men," and give silver, gold, and clothing. Pharaoh's heart is hardened and they pursue Israel into the sea, where they are confused, acknowledge the LORD fights for Israel, and are covered by the returning waters, seen dead on the shore.

afflict children of Israel [set over them with burdens] Pharaoh's taskmasters receive his command and tell the people that no straw will be given. They press the people urgently to fulfill the daily quota as when there was straw, and they beat the Israelite officers when it is not met.

Shiphrah and Puah, Hebrew midwives, feared God and defied the Egyptian king's order to kill newborn Hebrew boys. Questioned by Pharaoh, they claimed the women gave birth too quickly; God rewarded them with families.

The LORD is the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob and of the Israelites, also called the God of the Hebrews, with the name I AM WHO I AM. Earlier the patriarchs knew him as God Almighty. He calls Israel his people and his firstborn son, and he is jealous, unique, and owner of all the earth. The records present him as a deity rather than a human figure, though he speaks, acts, and is even seen. He is merciful, gracious, slow to anger, and abounding in loving kindness, yet he does not clear the guilty. The most important points are his covenant faithfulness, his deliverance of Israel from Egypt, and his demand for exclusive worship and obedience. The account begins with him rewarding the midwives who feared him and hearing Israel's groaning, remembering his covenant. He calls Moses from the bush, promises his presence, and commissions him. Against Pharaoh he hardens the king's heart, sends signs and plagues (frogs, flies, pestilence, boils, hail, locusts, darkness), and distinguishes Israel from Egypt. He executes judgment on the gods of Egypt and kills all the firstborn, and the Passover is established. He then leads Israel with a pillar of cloud and fire, divides the sea, and overthrows the Egyptian army. The song praises him as a man of war and an eternal king, and he heals Marah's waters. He provides manna, quail, and water from the rock, and pledges war on Amalek. At Sinai he offers a covenant, a kingdom of priests and a holy nation, descends in fire, and speaks the commandments. He gives laws on justice, worship, and the care of widows, orphans, and the poor, and promises an angel and the gradual driving out of Canaan's peoples. After the people corrupt themselves with the calf, he threatens to consume them as stiff-necked, relents at Moses' plea, and promises his presence. He speaks with Moses face to face, though no one can see his face and live, and he proclaims his name and renews the covenant. The later chapters turn to his detailed commands for the tabernacle, priestly garments, and rites, and for the Sabbath. He fills Bezalel, Oholiab, and the wise-hearted workers with wisdom. The work is completed as he commanded, and his glory fills the tabernacle, with his cloud guiding Israel's journeys.

l: Hebrew baby boys (sons born to Hebrew women), Exodus
s: is_ordered_to_be killed [by Pharaoh's command] The king of Egypt ordered the midwives to kill the boys at birth while letting the daughters live, but the midwives saved the boys alive. Pharaoh then commanded that every son born be cast into the river.

l: river (the Nile waters of Egypt), Exodus
s: has_state foul [after turned to blood] The river is where Pharaoh goes out to the water in the morning and where Moses is to meet him. Struck with the rod, its waters turn to blood, its fish die, and it becomes foul and undrinkable.

The forced labor of Israelites is hard service imposed by the Egyptians, consisting of mortar, brick, and field work that made their lives bitter. Taskmasters afflicted them with burdens, building Pithom and Raamses for Pharaoh, yet the people multiplied. Their bondage outlasted the king's death, and their groaning reached God, who heard. He promised to bring them out and redeem them, though cruel bondage kept them from heeding Moses.

Moses is a Hebrew born to Amram and Jochebed of the house of Levi. Hidden as an infant and set in a basket by the river, he is drawn out of the water by Pharaoh's daughter, who adopts him and names him. As an adult he kills an Egyptian striking a Hebrew and flees to Midian, where he helps Reuel's daughters, marries Zipporah, and has sons Gershom and Eliezer. He keeps Jethro's flock, his father-in-law's, until the LORD speaks from the burning bush at Horeb and sends him to Pharaoh and the elders of Israel. Moses objects that he is slow of speech and has uncircumcised lips, so the LORD appoints his brother Aaron as spokesman. Carrying God's rod, he returns toward Egypt; the LORD nearly kills him until Zipporah circumcises their son. At eighty he is made as God to Pharaoh and, with Aaron, delivers the LORD's demands. He prays to remove the frogs, flies, locusts, hail and thunder, performs the wonders, and is regarded as very great in Egypt. He instructs the elders in the Passover, takes Joseph's bones, and leads Israel out. He stretches his hand over the sea to divide it, and the people believe in the LORD and in him. In the wilderness he sings the victory song, sweetens the water at Marah, relays the manna rules, strikes the rock (naming Massah and Meribah), and holds up his hand so Israel prevails over Amalek. He builds an altar, and on Jethro's advice appoints rulers to share judging. At Sinai he is the mediator and sole approacher of the LORD. The frightened people ask him to speak for them. He sanctifies the people, writes the book of the covenant, seals it with blood, and stays forty days and nights on the mountain, where he receives instructions for the tabernacle, the priesthood, and the Sabbath. When the people make the calf, he intercedes, breaks the tablets, destroys the calf, and has the sons of Levi kill; he offers to be blotted out for the people. He speaks with the LORD face to face in the Tent of Meeting and asks to see his glory. He returns with new tablets and a shining face, which he veils. He directs Bezalel and Oholiab in the work, blesses the people for finishing it as commanded, and sets up the tabernacle exactly as told. The story ends with the LORD's glory filling it, so that Moses cannot enter the Tent of Meeting.

l: Moses' mother (woman of the house of Levi), Exodus
s: A daughter of Levi, married to a Levite man, she hides her fine son three months, then sets him in a tar-coated papyrus basket among reeds, and is finally hired by Pharaoh's daughter to nurse him.
She stands far off to watch what will happen to the baby in the basket. When Pharaoh's daughter finds him, she offers to fetch a Hebrew nurse and, told to go, brings the child's mother.
Pharaoh's daughter, attended by a servant and maidens, finds a crying Hebrew baby in a basket at the river, shows compassion, hires his mother as nurse, adopts him, and names him Moses.

The baby is identified as one of the Hebrews' children, and Hebrew women are the source of a possible nurse. Moses sees their burdens and sees an Egyptian strike a Hebrew. The next day two Hebrews fight each other, and the one in the wrong challenges Moses' authority and reveals knowledge of the killing.
He is seen striking a Hebrew, one of Moses' brothers. Moses kills him when no one is watching and hides his body in the sand.
Reuel is the priest of Midian and father of seven daughters, owner of a flock. After they report an Egyptian's help, he invites the man to eat bread and gives his daughter Zipporah to Moses.
Zipporah, Reuel's daughter, is given to Moses as wife and bears a son, Gershom, whom Moses names.

l: covenant (the LORD's covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob), Exodus
s: The LORD says he established his covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob to give them the land of Canaan, where they lived as aliens. He says he has remembered it on hearing Israel's groaning, and it grounds his promise to bring Israel into the land he swore to give them.

l: Moses' killing of the Egyptian, Exodus
s: Moses kills an Egyptian beating a Hebrew and buries him in sand; when a rebuked Hebrew reveals the deed is known, Pharaoh seeks Moses' death, and Moses flees to Midian.

Jethro is a priest of Midian and Moses' father-in-law. After hearing of God's deliverance of Israel, he brings Zipporah and her sons to Moses, declares the LORD greater than all gods, offers sacrifices, advises Moses to share judging, and then returns to his own land.

Mount Sinai, also called Horeb and God's Mountain, is holy ground where the LORD meets Moses. It first appears when Moses arrives with the flock and God promises that Israel will serve him there after leaving Egypt. Later Israel camps below; bounds are set, and touching the mountain means death. The LORD descends in fire and cloud as it smokes and quakes. Moses builds an altar with twelve pillars at its base, enters the cloud, and stays forty days and nights. He is later told to present himself alone on the top, where the LORD proclaims his name, and Moses descends with the tablets.
has_state burning but not consumed The bush burns with fire in which the LORD's angel appears, yet it is not consumed. It draws Moses to look, and God calls to him from the middle of it.

Canaan is the good, large land flowing with milk and honey that God promises the Israelites. It is inhabited by Canaanites, Hittites, Amorites, Perizzites, Hivites and Jebusites. First promised as their destination, it is then identified as the land sworn to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob's offspring, its peoples to be driven out.

The Canaanites are one of several peoples inhabiting the land Israel is entering. The LORD promises to drive them out; Israel must make no covenant with them and destroy their altars, pillars and Asherah poles, lest idolatry ensnare Israel.

is the LORD [memorial to all generations] When Moses asks what name to give, God says 'I AM WHO I AM' and tells him to say 'I AM has sent me to you.' God also says he is the LORD, the God of the fathers, and that this is his name forever and his memorial to all generations.

Aaron is a Levite, son of Amram and Jochebed, husband of Elisheba, and father of Nadab, Abihu, Eleazar, and Ithamar. He is Moses' brother, described by the LORD as a good speaker who will be Moses' mouth to the people. The records follow him from spokesman to priest. First, he meets Moses on God's mountain, speaks the LORD's words to the elders, and performs the signs. At eighty-three he goes with Moses to Pharaoh as prophet and speaker, and his rod becomes a serpent that swallows the magicians' rods. With the rod he brings plagues: blood in the waters, frogs, and lice. He accompanies Moses again for the locust warning. In the wilderness the murmuring people address him with Moses, and he lays up a pot of manna before the Testimony. He goes up the mountain with Nadab, Abihu, and seventy elders and sees the God of Israel. Moses then leaves him with Hur to settle disputes. The central thread is his appointment to the priesthood. With his sons he keeps the lamp from evening to morning as a statute forever. He is clothed in holy garments and bears Israel's names on his shoulders and heart. He wears the gold plate that bears the iniquity of the holy things so the people are accepted. He is washed, anointed, and consecrated for seven days, burns incense morning and evening, and makes yearly atonement at the altar's horns. He and his sons must wash at the basin so they do not die. The major failure is the golden calf. He collects the people's golden earrings, fashions the calf, builds an altar before it, and proclaims a feast to the LORD. When Moses confronts him, he blames the people and says the calf simply came out of the fire. The text says he let the people lose control. At the close, the LORD commands that he be brought to the Tent of Meeting, washed, clothed, and anointed to minister as priest, and he washes his hands and feet at the basin with Moses and his sons.

The rod is a sign-working staff carried by Moses as God's rod. In Chapter 4 it becomes a snake when thrown down and a rod again when grasped by the tail, showing the LORD has appeared. In Chapter 7, as Aaron's rod, it becomes a serpent before Pharaoh, swallows the magicians' rods, and strikes the river, turning the waters to blood.

purpose make Israelites believe the LORD appeared to Moses The LORD gives Moses three signs so that the people will believe: the rod turning into a snake, the hand turning leprous and then restored, and river water becoming blood on dry land. Moses tells Aaron about them, and Aaron performs them before the people, who believe.

l: blood plague (water turned to blood), Exodus
s: A plague in which the LORD strikes the river, turning Egypt's waters to blood, even in wood and stone vessels. Fish die, the river stinks, Egyptians cannot drink, magicians replicate it, and it lasts seven days.

l: officers of the children of Israel, Exodus
s: are_set_over Israelites (the people) [appointed by Pharaoh's taskmasters] The Israelite officers, set over the people by Pharaoh's taskmasters, are beaten and questioned about the missed quota. They cry out to Pharaoh, are rebuffed, and then tell Moses and Aaron that the LORD should look at them and judge, because they have made the officers a stench to Pharaoh and his servants.

is_withheld_by Pharaoh [people must gather their own] Pharaoh orders that straw no longer be supplied for making brick and that the people gather it themselves. The people are scattered across Egypt to gather stubble for straw, and the officers complain that none is given to them.

has_quota unchanged number [not diminished despite no straw] Pharaoh insists the number of bricks not be diminished even without straw provided. Failure to meet the daily quota leads to beatings of the Israelite officers, and Pharaoh repeats the demand to deliver the same number.

l: feast and sacrifice to the LORD, Exodus
s: is_requested_by Moses [to be held in the wilderness] Moses and Aaron ask that the people be allowed a three-day journey into the wilderness to hold a feast and sacrifice to the LORD, lest he fall on them with pestilence or the sword. Pharaoh rejects the request and treats the people's desire to sacrifice as evidence of idleness.

Wise men and sorcerers summoned by Pharaoh who use enchantments to imitate signs: they match rods-to-serpents, water-to-blood and frogs, though Aaron's rod swallows theirs, and they fail at lice, leaving Pharaoh hardened.

Pharaoh's hardened heart is a recurring condition in which the LORD foretells and causes Pharaoh's stubbornness. It follows the serpent sign and blood plague, then the boils. After the hail, Pharaoh hardens his own heart, and his servants do too. Throughout, he does not listen and does not release Israel, as the LORD spoke through Moses.

A plague threatened by the LORD against Egypt: at Aaron's gesture frogs rise from rivers and fill homes and beds; magicians copy it, but at Moses' prayer they die in stinking heaps, and Pharaoh hardens his heart.
The plague of lice strikes Egypt when Aaron strikes the dust and it becomes lice on man and animal; the magicians cannot imitate it, call it God's finger, yet Pharaoh stays hardened.

The plague of flies: the LORD sends swarms that corrupt Egypt's land and fill houses while sparing Goshen as a division sign; Pharaoh bargains, flies vanish at Moses' prayer, yet Pharaoh refuses again.

belongs_to Egypt [all of it died in the fifth plague] Egypt's livestock, including horses, donkeys, camels, herds and flocks, all die on the day the LORD appointed, while none of Israel's livestock die. Livestock left in the field later suffer under the hail, while those brought into houses are sheltered.

affects livestock (Egypt's livestock) [sent by the LORD; Israelite livestock spared] The LORD warns Pharaoh that a very grievous pestilence will strike the livestock in the field and sets the time for the next day. All of Egypt's livestock die, but not one of Israel's. Pharaoh sends to check and finds this true, yet he does not release the people.

The sixth plague: Moses sprinkles furnace ashes toward the sky before Pharaoh, they become dust causing boils on people and animals throughout Egypt; magicians cannot stand before Moses, and the LORD hardens Pharaoh's heart.

The seventh plague, an unprecedented hail in Egypt. The LORD warns a day ahead to shelter people and livestock; it then strikes with thunder and lightning, destroying people, animals, plants, trees, flax and barley, sparing Goshen and unripe wheat and spelt, and stops when Moses spreads his hands.

has_property unprecedented severity [no such locusts before or after] The locusts are brought by an east wind after Moses stretches out his rod, and they spread over all Egypt's borders, darkening the land. They eat every herb and all the fruit of the trees left by the hail, and are then driven into the Red Sea by a strong west wind, leaving none.

affects Egypt [covered land and ate all green plants] The plague of locusts is announced by Moses and Aaron as the result of Pharaoh's refusal, and is described as unparalleled before or after. It prompts Pharaoh to confess sin and ask for its removal, but after it ends the LORD hardens Pharaoh's heart and Israel is not released.

has_property palpable [thick darkness over Egypt for three days] The LORD commands Moses to stretch his hand toward the sky to bring a thick darkness that can be felt over Egypt for three days. No one in Egypt sees another or rises from his place, while Israel has light in its dwellings.

The Red Sea is a body of water that receives locusts driven by a west wind. It lies before Israel's camp at Pihahiroth. Its waters are driven back by an east wind, letting Israel cross on dry land as walls stand either side. The waters then return, drowning Pharaoh's army, and Moses leads Israel onward.

The plague of the firstborn is the final plague on Pharaoh and Egypt, announced for midnight when the LORD goes out through Egypt; all Egyptian firstborn die, causing a great cry and Pharaoh thrusting Israel out.

The firstborn of Egypt, from Pharaoh's heir to the servant's and the captive's, plus livestock, are the target of a foretold judgment. In Chapter 11 their death is announced, with Israel's people and animals spared. In Chapter 12 the LORD strikes them at midnight, leaving no Egyptian house without a dead.

The Passover is a perpetual ordinance and feast to the LORD, kept through generations, commemorating the Exodus from Egypt. Named for the LORD passing over Israelite houses, it is eaten in haste in one house with unleavened bread and bitter herbs, explained to children. Foreigners and hired servants are excluded; circumcised servants and strangers may eat; nothing remains until morning.

Each household takes an unblemished year-old male lamb from the sheep or goats on the tenth day, keeps it until the fourteenth, and kills it at evening. It is roasted whole with its head, legs, and inner parts, none of it left until morning, and none of its bones broken.

l: blood of the lamb (Passover lamb), Exodus
s: The blood is put on the two door posts and lintel of the houses where the lamb is eaten, applied with a bunch of hyssop from the basin. It serves as a token, so that when the LORD sees it he passes over the house and does not let the destroyer enter.

The Feast of Unleavened Bread is a seven-day observance held in the month Abib, commemorating the LORD bringing Israel's armies out of Egypt. Across the records, it requires eating unleavened bread, with no yeast or leavened bread in houses or within Israel's borders; anyone eating leavened bread is cut off from Israel. The first and seventh days are holy convocations with no work except food preparation, and a feast to the LORD falls on the seventh day. It is kept forever, yearly in the land, explained to sons, and no one appears before God empty-handed.

The Exodus from Egypt is Israel's departure from bondage, occurring in the month of Abib at the end of 430 years, to the day. After the firstborn were struck, Israel was thrust out in haste from Rameses to Succoth, carrying unleavened dough, plunder, flocks, herds, and a mixed multitude. It is to be observed as a night to the LORD and remembered with signs. God avoided the Philistine road, leading them by the wilderness toward Etham.

Firstborn is the law that the LORD claims every firstborn that opens the womb, human and animal, as his. Male animals belong to him; firstborn donkeys are redeemed with a lamb or have necks broken; human firstborn sons are redeemed, commemorating Egypt's firstborn killed.

The pillar of cloud is the form in which the LORD leads Israel by day and never departs from the people. At the Red Sea crossing it moves behind Israel, with the angel of God, separating them from Egypt's camp; it is dark yet gives light by night, and the LORD looks through it to confuse the Egyptian army. Later it descends to the Tent of Meeting door whenever Moses enters, as the LORD speaks with him and the people worship.
The pillar of fire is the form in which the LORD goes before Israel by night, giving light for day-and-night travel; it stays with the children of Israel and never departs from them.

Pharaoh's army, including six hundred chosen chariots, all the chariots of Egypt, horsemen, and captains, pursues Israel and overtakes them by the sea. In the sea the LORD confuses the army and takes off the chariot wheels, so they flee. The waters return and cover the chariots and horsemen so that not one of them remains. The Egyptian army, including Pharaoh's horses, chariots, horsemen, and chosen captains, is overwhelmed when the LORD brings the sea waters back on them. They sink like a stone and like lead in the mighty waters. The song depicts their intent to pursue, overtake, and divide plunder as defeated.

A miraculous event in which, at the LORD's command, Moses stretches his hand over the sea and a strong east wind all night divides it. Israel crosses on dry ground between walls of water; the Egyptians follow, and the returning waters drown them.
Miriam, a prophetess and Aaron's sister, takes a tambourine, leads the women out dancing, and answers them by repeating the song praising the LORD's triumph.

The song is sung by Moses and the children of Israel to the LORD. It praises his triumph over the horse and rider in the sea, declares him incomparable among the gods, and foretells that he will bring his people to his sanctuary while neighboring peoples tremble. It ends with the declaration that the LORD will reign forever and ever, and Miriam repeats its opening line.

Marah is a wilderness place reached after three days without water; its bitter, undrinkable waters give it its name. The LORD shows Moses a tree that sweetens them, and a statute is made and the people tested.

Manna is a bread given by the LORD, named by the house of Israel. It appears after the dew on the wilderness surface, white like coriander seed and tasting like wafers with honey. Each person gathers an omer; leftovers spoil except before the Sabbath, and it melts in the sun. An omer is preserved, and the people eat it forty years.
The wilderness of Sin is a place between Elim and Sinai, reached by the congregation on the fifteenth day of the second month after Egypt, where they murmur about hunger and receive quail and manna.

The Sabbath is the seventh day, a holy day of solemn rest to the LORD. It is presented as a sign between the LORD and Israel throughout generations and as a perpetual covenant. It commemorates creation: the LORD made heaven, earth, and sea in six days, rested on the seventh, blessed it, and made it holy. In Chapter 16 it appears through manna: the people gather twice as much on the sixth day, it does not spoil, none is found on the seventh, and they stay in their places and rest. Chapter 20 commands remembering and keeping it holy, with six days of labor and no work by household, servants, livestock, or the stranger within the gates. Chapter 31 calls it a sign that the LORD sanctifies Israel and makes profaning it punishable by death. Chapter 35 repeats the death penalty for working and forbids kindling fire in any habitation.

directed_against The LORD [not against Moses and Aaron] The people murmur against Moses and Aaron over hunger, saying they wish they had died in Egypt. Moses declares the murmurings are really against the LORD, who hears them and responds by promising and then providing meat and bread.

was_defeated_by Joshua [with the edge of the sword] Amalek comes and fights with Israel at Rephidim, prevailing whenever Moses lets down his hand. Joshua defeats Amalek and his people with the sword, and the LORD declares he will blot out the memory of Amalek and have war with Amalek from generation to generation.
Joshua, son of Nun, is Moses' young servant and companion who stays at the Tent; Moses commands him to choose men and fight Amalek, and he defeats them by the sword.

has_lack_of water [no water for the people to drink] Rephidim is where Israel encamps and finds there is no water for the people to drink. It is where the people quarrel with Moses, where the rock provides water, and where Amalek comes and fights with Israel.
A rock in Horeb where the LORD stands before Moses; Moses is told to strike it, and it yields water for the people to drink.

There is no water at Rephidim, and the thirsty people blame Moses for bringing them out to die of thirst with their children and livestock. The LORD provides water from the rock Moses strikes, so that the people may drink.

occurs_at Rephidim Amalek attacks Israel at Rephidim, and Joshua leads chosen men against them while Moses, Aaron, and Hur go up the hill. Israel prevails when Moses holds up his hand and Amalek prevails when he lets it down, so Aaron and Hur hold his hands steady until sunset. Joshua defeats Amalek with the edge of the sword.

is_between children of Israel [quarreled with Moses] Lacking water at Rephidim, the people quarrel with Moses, demand water, and accuse him of bringing them out of Egypt to kill them with thirst. Moses asks why they quarrel and test the LORD, cries out to the LORD, and the place is named Massah and Meribah because of the quarreling and testing.

l: judges and rulers (appointed by Moses), Exodus
s: Judges and rulers are able men chosen by Moses from all Israel, God-fearing, truthful, hating unjust gain. Organized as rulers of thousands, hundreds, fifties and tens, they judge at all times, handling small matters and sending hard cases to Moses.

was_performed_by Moses [alone, from morning to evening, before the counsel] Moses sits to judge the people from morning to evening, teaching them God's statutes and laws as they bring him their matters. Jethro calls this too heavy for one man, and the work is restructured so that rulers judge small matters and only hard or great cases go to Moses.

l: Jethro's counsel on delegating judgment, Exodus
s: Jethro's counsel to Moses, meant to ease his load so he can endure: judging alone will exhaust him and the people, so he should represent them before God, teach laws, and appoint able, God-fearing rulers; Moses follows it.

l: elders (of the people of Israel), Exodus
s: represent children of Israel [Moses called them to hear the LORD's words] The seventy elders are told to worship from a distance and later go up with Moses, Aaron, Nadab, and Abihu. They see the God of Israel, are not harmed, and eat and drink. Moses tells them to wait for his return, with Aaron and Hur available to settle disputes.

l: covenant (between the LORD and Israel), Exodus
s: The covenant is the agreement the LORD makes with the people of Israel concerning all his words. It begins with his offer: obedience and covenant-keeping will make them his own possession, a kingdom of priests and a holy nation, and the people agree. It is then established when they promise obedience, the book is read, offerings are made, and Moses seals it with blood.

The theophany at Sinai is the LORD's promised descent upon Mount Sinai on the third day, intended so the people would hear him speak with Moses and believe Moses forever. Announced beforehand, it arrives that morning with thunders, lightnings, thick cloud, loud trumpet, fire, smoke and a quaking mountain. The people tremble; God answers Moses by voice, while bounds and warnings keep people and priests from breaking through.

The commandments are spoken by God and include: no other gods, no idols, no misuse of the LORD's name, remembering the Sabbath, honoring father and mother, and prohibitions on murder, adultery, stealing, false testimony, and coveting. They cover duties toward God and toward neighbors, and some carry stated consequences or promises, such as long days in the land for honoring parents.

is_forbidden_by the Ten Commandments [no idol or image of anything in heaven, earth or water] God forbids making an idol or any image of anything in the heavens, on the earth, or in the water, and forbids bowing to or serving them. Later he specifically forbids making gods of silver or gold to be alongside him.
The altar is a worship structure the LORD prescribes: built of earth for burnt and peace offerings, or of uncut stone since tools pollute it, and without steps so nakedness is not exposed.

A Hebrew servant is bought by a master and serves six years, going out free in the seventh without payment, taking his wife if he came married. A wife given by the master stays with her children. If he declares love for his household, his ear is bored and he serves forever.

A master who owns a Hebrew servant under law. He must free the servant in the seventh year but keeps the wife he gave him and her children. If the servant refuses freedom, the master bores his ear with an awl at the door, binding him forever. He must also let a displeasing female servant be redeemed.

A daughter sold as a female servant, whose release differs from male servants. If her master is displeased with her, she may be redeemed but never sold to foreigners; if married to his son, she is treated as a daughter. If denied food, clothing or marital rights, she goes free without payment.
The chapter begins by introducing the ordinances that are to be set before the people. They cover servants, homicide and injury, retaliation, and liability for animals and pits.

l: servitude and release of servants, Exodus
s: Servitude terms are limited: Hebrew male servants go free in the seventh year, and female servants have protections regarding redemption and support. Injuring a servant's eye or tooth requires the master to free the servant. The permanent-service ear-boring rite is the exception for a servant who chooses to stay.

Chapter 21 sets penalties for homicide and violence: killing, striking or cursing parents, and kidnapping bring death; unintentional killers get a place of flight, schemers are taken even from the altar; non-fatal fights require compensation; a master killing a servant is punished unless the servant survives.

Male servants and maids are legally treated as their master's property. A master who beats a servant to death is punished, but not if the servant recovers within a day or two. Destroying an eye or tooth frees the servant. If a bull gores a servant, thirty silver shekels go to the master.

Lex talionis is a retributive principle in Chapter 21: if a pregnant woman is hurt in a fight and harm follows, life is taken for life, followed by a list of equal-for-equal penalties from eye to bruise.

penalty stoned [when it gores a man or woman to death; its meat shall not be eaten] A bull that gores a man or woman to death is stoned and its meat is not eaten. If it was known to gore before, the bull is stoned and its owner is also put to death. A bull that kills another's bull leads to selling the live one and dividing the price and the carcass.

A bull's owner bears liability only if the animal was known to gore and he failed to restrain it. Then he faces death, though ransom may replace it; a servant's death costs thirty silver shekels to the master, and a slain animal requires bull-for-bull replacement.

l: liability for animals and property, Exodus
s: Liability for animals and property in Chapter 21: a man who leaves a pit uncovered pays the owner when a bull or donkey falls in, keeping the carcass. When one bull kills another, the living bull and carcass are divided, unless it was known to gore, then bull for bull; killing a servant costs thirty shekels.

A thief is a legal figure in Chapter 22 whose liability depends on circumstances: killing or selling a stolen ox or sheep costs five oxen or four sheep, while a live animal found with him costs double. A night burglar's killer bears no bloodguilt, but after sunrise does. Unable to repay, the thief is sold.
must_not_be wronged or oppressed [because Israel were aliens in Egypt] The alien is not to be wronged or oppressed. The reason given is that the people were themselves aliens in the land of Egypt.

must_not_be taken advantage of [command] Widows and fatherless children must not be taken advantage of. If they cry out to the LORD, he will hear and respond with wrath, killing the oppressors with the sword so that their own wives become widows and their children fatherless.

The neighbor is a fellow member of the community who may entrust money, goods, or animals to another for keeping, or do so himself. His protections are set out by circumstance: he receives double from a found thief, is owed restitution for animals let loose in his field, and a borrower must repay an injured animal unless the owner was present. A keeper's oath before the LORD frees him from restitution.

includes ox, donkey, sheep [double payment if found alive] Oxen, sheep, and donkeys are the main stolen property in these laws, with penalties of fivefold, fourfold, or double depending on whether they were killed or sold or found alive. Animals that are lost, injured, or die while kept by a neighbor are handled by oath or restitution. Animals torn by wild beasts need not be replaced if the torn carcass is brought as evidence, but the meat of such animals must not be eaten and is cast to the dogs. Firstborn livestock stay with the mother seven days and are given to the LORD on the eighth.

A body of laws on theft and restitution, set out in Chapter 22. It fixes repayment from double to five times for theft, damage by animals or fire, and lost borrowed goods, with disputes brought before God, then turns to seduction, dowries, and bans on interest and overnight pledges.

The angel is sent before the Israelites to keep them on the way and bring them to the prepared place, and to bring them in to the peoples of the land. The people must listen to his voice and not provoke him, since he will not pardon disobedience and God's name is in him.

A collective of peoples inhabiting the land, Amorites, Hittites, Perizzites, Canaanites, Hivites, Jebusites, who may not dwell among the Israelites lest they cause sin; they are to be driven out gradually, with no covenant made.

is_a snare [for Israelites who serve them] The Israelites are told not to invoke the names of other gods, bow down to them, serve them, or make a covenant with them. Their pillars are to be demolished, and serving them would be a snare.

l: justice and fair testimony laws, Exodus
