s: Laws on justice and honest testimony: they forbid false reports, malicious witnessing, bribes that blind and pervert, crowd-driven injustice, partiality, denying the poor justice, and killing the innocent, require helping an enemy's animals, and ban oppressing aliens, who Israelites once were.

occurs_in seventh year [land rests and lies fallow for the poor] The land is to be sown and harvested for six years and left to rest and lie fallow in the seventh. The poor of the people eat what grows, and animals of the field eat what they leave. The same applies to vineyards and olive groves.
Sabbath rest is a weekly observance on the seventh day after six days of work, letting oxen, donkeys, servants' sons and aliens rest and be refreshed.

celebrates first fruits [of labors sown in the field] The feast of harvest is the feast of the first fruits of the Israelites' labors, which they sow in the field. It is one of three yearly feasts at which all males appear before the Lord GOD.

occurs_at end of the year [when labors are gathered from the field] The feast of ingathering is held at the end of the year, when the Israelites gather in their labors from the field. It is one of three yearly feasts at which all males appear before the Lord GOD.
Moses writes all the LORD's words and takes this book to read in the hearing of the people. After hearing it, the people say they will do all that the LORD has said and be obedient.

is_a sign of the covenant [sprinkled on the people] Moses puts half of the blood from the peace offerings in basins and sprinkles half on the altar. He then sprinkles the blood on the people and declares it the blood of the covenant that the LORD has made with them concerning all these words.

l: two tablets of the covenant, Exodus
s: Two stone tablets of the covenant, containing law and commands, written by the LORD with God's finger and given to Moses on Mount Sinai after he finished speaking with Him.

The offering for the tabernacle work is commanded by the LORD and taken from the children of Israel, only from those whose hearts make them willing. Chapter 25 lists its materials: metals, dyed fabrics, skins, acacia wood, oil, spices, and stones. Chapter 35 repeats the command, and the people bring it freely, women spinning and rulers bringing stones, spices, and oil.

The tabernacle, also called the Tent of Meeting and the Tabernacle of the Testimony, is a sanctuary the LORD commands the people to make so that he may dwell among them. It and all its furniture must follow the pattern he shows Moses on the mountain. Its structure is ten curtains of fine twined linen with cherubim, coupled into a single unit by gold clasps and loops. Acacia wood boards stand upright on silver sockets and are held by gold-overlaid bars, with bronze pins. It is covered by eleven goats' hair curtains, then rams' skins dyed red, with sea cow hides above. A veil of blue, purple, scarlet and linen divides the holy place from the most holy place, and an embroidered screen hangs at the tent door. Inside, the ark of the covenant stands screened by the veil, the table of showbread on the north side, the lamp stand opposite on the south, and the golden incense altar before the veil. The altar of burnt offering is at the door, with a basin between it and the tent, and a court with a screened gate surrounds it. The account unfolds from command to making to completion. Chapters 25 and 26 give the command and design, and chapter 35 lists the parts and furnishings. In chapter 36 wise-hearted workers build it, and in chapter 38 its materials are counted under Ithamar for the Levites' service, with Bezalel making everything commanded. In chapter 39 the work is declared finished, and the Israelites bring it to Moses, who sees it was done as commanded. In chapter 40 it is raised on the first day of the first month of the second year, furnished and enclosed by the court. Then the cloud covers it and the LORD's glory fills it.

The ark of the covenant is a chest of acacia wood, two and a half cubits long and a cubit and a half wide and high, overlaid inside and outside with pure gold, with a gold molding, four gold rings in its feet, and gold-overlaid acacia poles that stay in the rings. It is first specified as a command, then built by Bezalel to those measures. Finally Moses puts the covenant inside, sets the poles, places the mercy seat above it, and brings it into the tabernacle's most holy place, screened by the veil as the LORD commanded.

The mercy seat is a pure gold cover, two and a half cubits long and a cubit and a half wide, set on top of the ark of the covenant. Chapter 25 prescribes it, with the LORD promising to meet Moses and speak from above it between two cherubim; Chapter 37 has Bezalel make it, cherubim formed as one piece.

Two cherubim of hammered gold are to be made of one piece with the mercy seat, one at each end. They spread their wings upward, covering the mercy seat, with their faces toward one another and toward the mercy seat. Bezalel makes two cherubim of beaten gold, one at each end of the mercy seat and of one piece with it. They spread their wings above, covering the mercy seat, with their faces toward one another and toward the mercy seat.

The table is a furnishing located on the north side of the tabernacle, outside the veil. It is made of acacia wood, two cubits long, a cubit wide and one and a half cubits high, overlaid with pure gold with a gold molding and hand-width rim. Four gold rings hold gold-overlaid carrying poles. Its pure gold vessels include dishes, spoons, bowls and pitchers. Chapter 25 gives instructions, including bread of the presence always set before the LORD; Chapter 37 has Bezalel make it.

The lamp stand is a tabernacle furnishing of pure hammered gold, made as one piece with base, shaft, cups, buds, and flowers, weighing a talent including all accessories. It has six branches, three per side, with almond-blossom cups, and seven lamps lighting the space in front of it, plus gold snuffers and snuff dishes. It stands on the south side, opposite the table. Chapter 25 gives the instructions; Chapter 37 shows Bezalel making it accordingly.

The ephod is a skillfully crafted garment made of gold, blue, purple, scarlet, and fine twined linen. It has two shoulder straps joined at the ends and a skillfully woven band of the same piece and materials, used to fasten it. Its most notable feature is the two onyx stones on the shoulder straps, engraved with the names of the children of Israel, six tribal names each, set in gold with braided chains, serving as memorial stones. Chapter 28 describes its design, including the breastplate bound with blue lace and an all-blue robe. Chapter 39 repeats the construction, adding gold beaten into thin plates and cut into wires.

The breastplate is a sacred garment piece made in the same work as the ephod, of gold, blue, purple, scarlet, and fine twined linen. It is square and folded double, a span by a span. Its most important feature is twelve stones, set in gold in four rows of three, each engraved with the name of one of the twelve tribes of Israel, so it represents the children of Israel. The Urim and the Thummim are placed in it. In Chapter 28 it is described as hanging by braided gold chains and rings, bound to the ephod with a blue lace, resting on Aaron's heart as a continual memorial before the LORD. Chapter 39 repeats the design as made, attached to the ephod's shoulder straps and rings so it stays on the woven band and does not come loose.

Anointing oil is a perfume compounded by a perfumer from myrrh, cinnamon, cane, cassia and a hin of olive oil. It sanctifies the Tent of Meeting, its furnishings, altars, basin, and Aaron and his sons for priesthood. It is forbidden on ordinary people's flesh and may not be imitated; offenders are cut off from their people.

l: curtains of fine twined linen (tabernacle's ten curtains), Exodus
s: Ten curtains of fine twined linen in blue, purple and scarlet, decorated with cherubim by a skillful workman, each 28 by 4 cubits. They are coupled in two sets of five, with fifty blue loops and fifty gold clasps joining them, so the tabernacle becomes a unit.

l: curtains of goats' hair (covering over the tabernacle), Exodus
s: Eleven goats' hair curtains, each thirty by four cubits, form a covering over the tabernacle. They are coupled in sets of five and six, joined by fifty loops on the outer edges and fifty bronze clasps. The sixth curtain is doubled at the tent front, the overhang hangs over back and sides, and rams' skins and sea cow hides go above.

The boards are the upright acacia-wood walls of the tabernacle, each ten cubits long and one and a half wide, with two tenons. Twenty stand on the south, twenty on the north, and eight on the west, including two corner boards. Each rests on two silver sockets, forty per long side and sixteen on the west. All are overlaid with gold and fitted with gold rings, and are held by acacia bars, five per side, the middle bar passing end to end.

The veil is a skillfully worked curtain of blue, purple, scarlet and fine twined linen decorated with cherubim. It hangs on four gold-overlaid acacia pillars set in silver sockets, separating the holy place from the most holy, near the ark of the covenant.

The altar is a square acacia-wood object, five cubits long and wide and three high, overlaid with bronze. Its horns rise from the four corners in one piece with it. It is built hollow with planks, as shown on the mountain, and has bronze vessels, a grating with four rings, and carrying poles.

The court is the enclosed space around the tabernacle, one hundred cubits long, fifty wide and five high. It is enclosed by fine twined linen hangings hung on pillars. Most important is its layout: the south and north sides run one hundred cubits with twenty pillars and twenty bronze sockets each, the west side is fifty cubits with ten pillars and sockets, and the east side is fifty cubits with the gate in the middle and fifteen-cubit hangings on each side. The pillars stand in bronze sockets, with silver hooks, fillets and overlaid capitals, and bronze pins. The gate is a twenty-cubit screen of blue, purple, scarlet and fine linen on four pillars. Chapter 27 prescribes it; Chapter 38 recounts its construction.

The tabernacle court's hangings are fine twined linen enclosing the court: 100 cubits on the south and north sides, 50 on the west, and 50 on the east split 15 cubits either side of the gate, hung on pillars with silver hooks and fillets and bronze sockets.
is_used_for lamp [beaten oil for light, burning continually] Pure olive oil, beaten for the light, is to be brought by the children of Israel so that a lamp may burn continually.

Aaron's sons (named as Nadab, Abihu, Eleazar, and Ithamar) are a group appointed to the priesthood to minister alongside Aaron. They keep the lamp in order from evening to morning in the Tent of Meeting, a statute forever throughout generations. They are given tunics, sashes or belts, headbands, and linen pants covering their flesh so they do not bear iniquity and die. The records unfold from their naming and clothing, to anointing, consecration, and sanctification with Aaron: laying hands on offerings, blood applied to ear, thumb, and toe, and sharing the consecration meal. Their priesthood is a perpetual statute, and one of them will wear Aaron's garments afterward. Finally they are brought to the door, washed, clothed, and anointed as their father was, and wash hands and feet when entering the Tent or approaching the altar.

The Tent of Meeting is both a sacred structure and a meeting place where the LORD meets and speaks with Moses and Israel. Its furnishings include the veil, ark of the covenant, table, pure lamp stand with vessels, altar of incense, altar of burnt offering, and basin with its base. The records begin with the lamp kept by Aaron and his sons outside the veil from evening to morning. They then describe its role in consecration: Aaron and his sons are washed, the bull is killed, the consecration meal is eaten, and the daily burnt offering is made at its door, where the LORD promises to meet Israel and sanctify it by his glory. Washing at the basin is required before entering, so they do not die. It is first to be anointed with holy oil, and incense is placed before the covenant where the LORD meets Moses. It is the first thing commanded to be made, with its furniture. Finally, Moses habitually pitches the tent far outside the camp; everyone seeking the LORD goes there, the pillar of cloud stands at its door as the LORD speaks with Moses, and the people worship from their tent doors.

l: holy garments (for Aaron and his sons), Exodus
s: The holy garments are the priestly vestments made for Aaron to minister in the priest's office, giving glory and beauty and sanctifying him. They include the breastplate of judgment, ephod, robe, fitted tunic, turban, and sash, with a gold plate of the holy crown inscribed "HOLY TO THE LORD" tied to the turban. Wise-hearted workers, filled by the LORD with wisdom, made them from gold, blue, purple, scarlet, and fine linen. Aaron's sons also receive tunics, sashes, headbands, and linen pants. Aaron is clothed in them for consecration, and they then pass to his sons for anointing; the successor priest wears them seven days upon entering the Tent of Meeting. The finished garments are brought to Moses with the tabernacle work.

The robe of the ephod is a garment of woven work, all blue, with a bound head opening so it won't tear. Its skirts bear pomegranates of blue, purple, scarlet and twined linen alternating with pure gold bells, whose sound is heard so Aaron does not die entering and leaving the holy place.

Priesthood ordination is the perpetual statute by which Aaron and his sons are set apart to minister to the LORD as priests. It begins with clothing in holy garments, anointing, consecration and sanctification, with linen pants required so they do not bear iniquity and die. It continues with their lasting portion of the wave offering and succession by Aaron's sons. It concludes with washing, clothing and anointing that grant an everlasting priesthood throughout their generations.

has_status most holy [after seven days of atonement and sanctification] The altar receives the bull's blood on its horns and the rams' blood sprinkled around it, and the fat and offerings are burned on it. It is to be cleansed, anointed, and atoned for over seven days until it is most holy, so that whatever touches it is holy. The daily lamb offerings are made on it, and the LORD says he will sanctify it.

l: bull (sin offering for Aaron's consecration), Exodus
s: is_a sin offering A young bull is brought to the Tent of Meeting, Aaron and his sons lay hands on its head, and it is killed before the LORD. Its blood is put on the altar's horns and poured at the base, its fat and organs are burned on the altar, and its meat, skin, and dung are burned outside the camp as a sin offering. A bull of sin offering is offered every day of the seven days for atonement.

l: burnt offering ram (first ram of consecration), Exodus
s: is_a burnt offering [offered whole on the altar] The first ram has hands laid on its head by Aaron and his sons and is killed. Its blood is sprinkled around the altar, and the ram is cut in pieces, with innards and legs washed, and burned whole on the altar as a burnt offering, a pleasant aroma to the LORD.

is_a ram of consecration The second ram has hands laid on it and is killed. Its blood is put on the right ear, thumb, and big toe of Aaron and his sons and sprinkled on the altar, and with oil on the priests and their garments. Its fat, right thigh, and one loaf, cake, and wafer are waved and burned, its breast is Aaron's portion, and its meat is boiled and eaten by the priests at the tent door, with leftovers burned by morning.

The consecration involves washing, clothing, and anointing, the sin offering bull, the burnt offering ram, and the ram of consecration with blood and oil applied to the priests. It lasts seven days, with daily atonement for the altar, and the meat and bread are eaten only by the priests, not by a stranger.

The daily continual burnt offering consists of two year-old lambs offered on the altar, one each morning and evening. Each lamb is accompanied by fine flour mixed with beaten oil and a wine drink offering. It is kept throughout the generations at the Tent of Meeting door, where the LORD meets Israel.

The altar of incense is a most holy object made of acacia wood, one cubit long and wide (square) and two cubits high, with horns of one piece with it. Its top, sides and horns are overlaid with pure gold, with a gold molding and two gold rings under the molding holding gold-overlaid carrying poles. It stands before the veil by the mercy seat, and only incense may be offered on it: no strange incense, burnt, meal or drink offerings. It is anointed with holy oil. Aaron makes atonement on its horns once yearly with sin offering blood. Bezalel builds it.

Holy incense is a perpetual offering before the LORD, burned on the altar each morning and evening. It combines equal weights of sweet spices, gum resin, onycha, galbanum and pure frankincense, salted. Some is beaten small and set before the covenant in the Tent of Meeting. Private imitation is forbidden; imitators are cut off.

The census ransom is a half-shekel payment, by the sanctuary shekel, made by every man aged twenty and up when the people are counted. Rich and poor pay equally. It atones for souls, prevents plague, and is appointed for the Tent of Meeting's service as a memorial.

A bronze basin with a bronze base, made from mirrors, set between the Tent of Meeting and the altar of burnt offering and filled with water. Aaron and his sons must wash their hands and feet in it before entering the Tent or approaching the altar, or they die. This is a statute forever; the basin is also anointed with holy oil.

The altar of burnt offering is a square, hollow acacia-wood structure, five cubits by five cubits and three cubits high, overlaid with bronze. It has one-piece horns on its four corners. It was fitted with a bronze grating, rings and bronze-covered carrying poles, plus bronze vessels. Its sockets, grating and vessels came from the offering bronze.

Bezalel is a craftsman of the tribe of Judah, son of Uri and grandson of Hur. The LORD calls him by name and fills him with the Spirit of God, giving him wisdom, understanding, knowledge and skill in workmanship: work in gold, silver and bronze, stone cutting and wood carving. He also has it in his heart to teach. Early on, his lineage, calling and gifts are announced. He is then named alongside Oholiab as one who works with the wise-hearted men to whom the LORD gave wisdom for the sanctuary work, and Moses calls him to that work. He goes on to build the sanctuary furnishings: the ark, the mercy seat of pure gold, two beaten-gold cherubim, the table and its vessels, the beaten-work lamp stand with seven lamps, snuffers and dishes, and the acacia-wood altar of incense. He also makes the holy anointing oil and pure incense of sweet spices. The records close by stating that he made all that the LORD commanded Moses.

Oholiab, son of Ahisamach of the tribe of Dan, is a skilled engraver, workman and embroiderer in blue, purple, scarlet and fine linen. The LORD appoints him to work with Bezalel, filling him with wisdom of heart for engraving, embroidery and weaving. Across the chapters he is first appointed (31), named with Bezalel as a teacher (35), called by Moses to labor with every wise-hearted man on the sanctuary according to the LORD's command (36), and finally shown working alongside Bezalel (38).

A molded gold calf Aaron made from the people's golden earrings. The people hailed it as the gods who brought them out of Egypt and made offerings. Moses then burned it, ground it to powder, scattered it on water, and made the Israelites drink it.

is_on_the_side_of LORD [gathered to Moses when called] All the sons of Levi gather to Moses when he calls for those on the LORD's side. They carry out his command to go through the camp with swords, and about three thousand men fall.
Tablets of the covenant, the work of God, engraved with his writing on both sides. Moses carries them down the mountain, then in anger at the calf and dancing throws them down and breaks them.

l: killing of about three thousand men, Exodus
s: is_carried_out_by sons of Levi [at Moses' command] At Moses' word, relaying the LORD's command, the sons of Levi go from gate to gate through the camp killing brother, companion, and neighbor. About three thousand men of the people fall that day. Moses then tells the Levites to consecrate themselves to the LORD so that he may give them a blessing.

l: Moses' request to see God's glory, Exodus
s: Moses, after the LORD agrees to go with them, asks to see his glory. The LORD answers that his goodness will pass before Moses and his name be proclaimed, but refuses to show his face. Hiding Moses in a rock cleft, he lets him see only his back.
A pair of chiseled stone tablets, replacing the broken first set, which Moses carries up, inscribes with the covenant's ten commandments, and brings down from Sinai.

The covenant is the LORD's agreement with Moses and Israel, promising marvels and driving out the land's inhabitants. Its terms forbid covenants with inhabitants and idols, and require exclusive worship, feasts, Sabbath and firstborn laws; the words are written on tablets as the ten commandments.

l: wise-hearted men (workers of the sanctuary), Exodus
s: receives_offerings_from Moses [offerings brought by Israelites for the sanctuary] These men, whose hearts the LORD filled with wisdom and stirred to come, receive the offerings and tell Moses the people have brought more than enough. They then make the tabernacle curtains, coverings, boards, sockets, bars, veil, and door screen with its pillars.

The sanctuary is the object of the service for which the LORD gave the workers wisdom, and the offerings are brought for its work. The work on it is carried out according to all that the LORD commanded.

quantity more than enough [sufficient for all the work, and too much] The offerings are received by the workers from Moses, and free will offerings keep coming every morning. They prove much more than enough, so Moses has the people stopped from bringing more, as the stuff was sufficient for all the work and too much.

has_amount twenty-nine talents and seven hundred thirty shekels [according to the shekel of the sanctuary] The gold used in all the work of the sanctuary, including the gold of the offering, totaled twenty-nine talents and seven hundred thirty shekels by the sanctuary shekel.

Silver collected from the counted men of the congregation totaled one hundred talents and 1,775 shekels by the sanctuary shekel, at a beka (half shekel) a head from each man twenty and older, 603,550 men. The hundred talents were cast into one hundred sockets for the sanctuary and veil; the 1,775 shekels made hooks, capitals and fillets for the pillars.

The bronze of the offering totaled seventy talents and 2,400 shekels. It was used for sockets at the Tent of Meeting door, the bronze altar with its grating and vessels, sockets around the court and its gate, and all pins of the tabernacle and court.

A cloud covering the tabernacle once the work is finished, barring Moses from entering; it rests there by day with fire visible to all Israel by night, and Israel travels when it lifts and stays when it rests.
Moses raises the tabernacle on the first day of the first month of the second year, as the LORD commanded, setting up each part and furnishing in turn and finishing with the court and gate screen.

This is the Book of Numbers, a narrative and legal record of Israel's organization at Sinai and forty years of wilderness travel to the edge of Canaan. Moses, Aaron and later Eleazar and Joshua lead under the LORD's direct commands. In the first part, at Sinai, Moses counts the fighting men (603,550), arranges the camps around the Tent of Meeting by tribal standards, and sets apart the Levites in place of the firstborn, assigning the clans of Gershon, Kohath and Merari their tabernacle duties. Laws on uncleanness, restitution, jealousy, Nazirite vows and the priestly blessing follow, then the princes' dedication offerings, the cleansing of the Levites, the Passover, and the guiding cloud and silver trumpets. The journey then turns to repeated rebellion. The people complain, crave meat and suffer a plague. Miriam and Aaron oppose Moses, and Miriam is struck with leprosy. After twelve spies explore Canaan, only Caleb and Joshua urge conquest. The people's refusal brings the decree that the adult generation will die in the wilderness over forty years. Korah's revolt ends with the earth swallowing the rebels and a plague, and Aaron's budding rod confirms the priesthood. Further rules cover offerings, the red heifer and tithes. Near the end of the wanderings Miriam and Aaron die, and Moses, having struck the rock, is barred from entering the land. Israel defeats Arad, Sihon and Og, and a bronze serpent heals those bitten by snakes. In Moab, Balak hires Balaam to curse Israel, but Balaam, after his donkey speaks, blesses Israel three times and foretells a star from Jacob. Israel then sins with Baal Peor, and Phinehas stops the plague and receives a covenant of peace. A second census (601,730) shows that only Caleb and Joshua survive from the first generation. The final chapters prepare for settlement. Zelophehad's daughters win inheritance rights, Joshua is commissioned to succeed Moses, and festival offerings and vow laws are set out. Israel avenges itself on Midian, Reuben, Gad and half of Manasseh settle east of the Jordan, and the journey's stages are recounted. The LORD gives the land's borders, appoints men to divide it, assigns Levite cities and cities of refuge, and rules that daughters' inheritances must stay within their tribe.

The LORD is the God of Israel, presented throughout these records as a deity who speaks, commands, dwells, judges and forgives. He is called the God of the spirits of all flesh, does not lie, and is slow to anger and abundant in loving kindness, forgiving iniquity yet not clearing the guilty. He speaks to Moses, his servant, mouth to mouth and plainly, while he reveals himself to other prophets by vision and dream. He sometimes also addresses Aaron and Eleazar. What matters most is his covenant relationship with Israel. He brought them out of Egypt to be their God, struck Egypt's firstborn, and executed judgments on the gods of Egypt. He claims Israel's firstborn and takes the Levites in their place, giving them to Aaron and his sons. He dwells in the midst of the camp and among the people, so the camp and the land must not be defiled. His presence is shown in the cloud and the pillar of cloud by day and fire by night, and his glory appears at the Tent of Meeting. He puts his name on the people through the priestly blessing. He promised and gives Canaan to Israel, and he commands them to drive out its inhabitants and destroy idols. The account unfolds from Sinai to the plains of Moab. At Sinai he orders censuses, the arrangement of the camp by standards, the Levites' duties, and laws on purity, vows, the Nazirite, offerings and Passover. He directs the people's travels by the cloud and silver trumpets. On the journey he responds to complaint with fire, quails, a plague, leprosy for Miriam, and the rebels' fate by earth and fire. He pardons at Moses' plea yet decrees that the complaining generation die in the wilderness over forty years. He sends serpents and then provides the bronze serpent and water. He declares Moses and Aaron will not enter the land, and he directs Aaron's death. Through Balaam he blesses Israel, saying he has not cursed them and sees no iniquity in them. He is angered by the Baal Peor sin and rewards Phinehas with a covenant of peace. In the closing chapters he commands vengeance on Midian, chooses Joshua, sets inheritance law for Zelophehad's daughters, defines the land's borders and its division by lot, and provides Levite cities and cities of refuge.

Moses is a person: the servant of the LORD and leader of the children of Israel through the wilderness, from Sinai to the plains of Moab. He is brother of Aaron and Miriam, son of Amram and Jochebed, married to a Cushite woman, and has Joshua as his servant. The records describe him as humble beyond all people on earth and faithful in the LORD's house, one with whom the LORD speaks mouth to mouth. His defining role is intermediary: he repeatedly receives the LORD's commands and relays them to Israel, Aaron, tribal heads, and others, and he carries them out. The account opens with the census at Sinai, the arrangement of the camp, the counting and assignment of the Levites, redemption of the firstborn, and rules on uncleanness, jealousy, Nazirite vows, and Passover. He sets up and anoints the tabernacle, gives wagons and oxen to the Levites, and hears the LORD from above the mercy seat. On the journey he invites Hobab to join them, prays when the ark moves and rests, and, burdened by the people, asks to be killed. He gathers seventy elders and wishes all the LORD's people were prophets. He intercedes for Miriam. He sends the twelve spies, and intercedes when the people murmur. He faces challenges, notably Korah's rebellion, and answers them with the censer test, and Aaron's budding rod confirms Aaron's priesthood. A turning point comes at the waters of Meribah in the wilderness of Zin, where he strikes the rock instead of speaking to it and is told he will not bring the assembly into the promised land. He still deals with Edom, Aaron's death, and the bronze serpent. Late in the account he is told to hold the census with Eleazar, to take the daughters' inheritance case to the LORD, and to go up Mount Abarim to see the land before being gathered to his people. He asks for a successor and commissions Joshua. He relays laws on feasts and vows, commissions the war on Midian, rebukes Reuben and Gad, and gives land east of the Jordan to Gad, Reuben, half of Manasseh, and Gilead to Machir. He records Israel's journeys, relays the borders and land division by lot, and rules that Zelophehad's daughters must marry within their father's tribe.

Aaron is the priest, head of the house of Levi, and father of four sons: Nadab (the firstborn), Abihu, Eleazar and Ithamar. Nadab and Abihu died for offering strange fire and left no children. Together with Moses he helped lead Israel out of Egypt, and the records follow him through the wilderness until his death. Early on he helps Moses count Israel's men and the Levites. The Levites are given to him and his sons to serve. He and his sons keep the priesthood and camp east of the tabernacle. They cover the sanctuary furniture, appoint the Kohathites to their burdens, and direct the Gershonites' service. At the LORD's command they bless the children of Israel with a three-part formula, and he lights the seven lamps and offers the Levites as a wave offering. His failings and his vindication follow. He joins Miriam in speaking against Moses and is rebuked, then confesses the sin and asks that it not be counted against them. When rebels complain against him, he takes his censer and incense, makes atonement, and stands between the dead and the living so that the plague stops. His rod alone sprouts, buds, blossoms and bears almonds, marking him as the LORD's chosen man. The priestly office is defined as a heavy duty with provision attached. He and his sons bear the iniquity of the sanctuary and guard the altar. They receive wave offerings, first fruits and the firstborn, which must be redeemed. He has no inheritance in the land, because the LORD is his portion and inheritance. His end comes at Meribah, where he joins Moses before the rock and is barred from the promised land because of the rebellion against the LORD's word. At the LORD's command he goes up Mount Hor, his garments are put on his son Eleazar, and he dies on the mountaintop on the first day of the fifth month in the fortieth year after the exodus, aged 123. All the house of Israel weeps for him thirty days.

The Tent of Meeting, also called the Tent of the Testimony, is the sacred tabernacle at the center of Israel's camp, where the LORD meets with Moses. Tribes camp around it at a distance, with Levite clans positioned on three sides and Moses, Aaron, and his sons to the east. It sets out after the second camp when the camps move, with the Levites in the middle. Once set up, anointed, and sanctified by Moses, it becomes the place of Levite service: Levites aged thirty to fifty carry and care for its holy things, furnishings, and coverings, and are presented and cleansed before it. Aaron's rod is laid before the covenant there and kept as a token. Throughout, strangers and ordinary Israelites may not approach it, on pain of death or bearing sin.

Egypt is the place the people wish they had died in and want to return to under a new leader. Moses says the Egyptians would hear of it if the LORD killed the people he brought out by his might. The LORD's signs were worked there.
